they are severed by two moments of mind at the stage of the diamond-like concentration. Answer: Because the initial wisdom of the path of seeing is inferior, the two obstacles are severed sequentially.
The power of the Vajra Path is strong;

the two obscurations are severed simultaneously. Question: Since the obscuration of meditative concentration is subsumed under the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is accepted that those of the Two Vehicles sever it through the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

"Is it not so? [He] replied, "It is. [The interlocutor asked: "If you admit that the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) is subtle while the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is coarse, and that the emptiness of persons eliminates the subtle cognitive obstructions (jñeya-āvaraṇa), then it would also follow that the emptiness of persons is coarse and the emptiness of phenomena is subtle."
When the grasping at the self of persons arises, it carries with it the grasping at phenomena; there is no understanding that would serve as an exception to this.
Furthermore, when comparing the grasping at persons to the grasping at phenomena, the grasping at phenomena is more subtle.
If one considers the grasping at birth in relation to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
the cognitive obscuration is indeed coarse. Why is this?
Because delusion regarding principles is subtle while delusion regarding phenomena is coarse,
when one realizes the nature of reality and severs the grasping at a self,
one is simultaneously able to sever those cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) concerning phenomena.
However, when observing dharmas in detail,
it must be accompanied by the observation of arising;
this observation of arising is coarse.
The statement that "the contemplation of non-associated phenomena" intends to refer to those associated with the delusion regarding principles is an incorrect interpretation;
for the hindrance of meditative concentration (samādhy-āvaraṇa) arises simultaneously with the afflictions that delude one regarding principles.
Do the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) also arise in association with delusion regarding the principles?
According to the sixth [chapter],
those that arise in conjunction with greed, hatred, views, and doubt [do so].
Furthermore, because they are deluded regarding the same principle and share the same object,
one should know by analogy that the hindrance of meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) should likewise be so;
since it arises simultaneously and shares the same delusion, it is subsumed under the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained through abandonment; it is an inferior experience that gives rise to distinct obstacles to meditative concentration,
which the followers of the Two Vehicles suppress but do not abandon.
Because it is subsumed under the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
when practitioners of the Two Vehicles suppress this hindrance to meditative concentration and attain the two meditative absorptions,
they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but do not attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Therefore, it cannot be objected that the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is coarse while being able to sever subtle obstacles, thereby causing the arising of the contemplation that brings along with it the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). [Objection:
The grasping at a self through conceptualization (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*) is coarse and thus easy to sever.
At the initial moment of seeing the path, one is able to eliminate [the afflictions].
Since the Mahāyāna has three moments of mind for seeing the path, how many does the Two Vehicles have? Answer: By inferring from the underlying principle.
In the Mahāyāna, each of the two obstacles is divided into two grades;
by severing them individually and collectively, three stages of mind are established.
This is because the second stage of mind severs only the lower grade of the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
If those of the two vehicles possess only two types of mind, it is because they sever only the two grades of self-clinging. Question: The two obstacles are divided into superior and inferior grades;
which two grades of mind are eliminated?
The two obstructions are divided into subtle and coarse;
the abandonment of the subtle is likewise divided into two. Answer: Because the power of the initial path is still inferior, it eliminates only the two types of lower-grade [afflictions].
Because the subsequent path possesses superior capacity, it eliminates [the afflictions] by means of a single mental application (*ekāgra-citta*).
Question: Why does the preceding section on the seven conditions and eight causes for the co-emergent grasping not mention "appropriation" (*upādāna*) as a distinction?
The intermittent view of self is said to be the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*). Answer: Seven [consciousnesses] take only the eighth as their object;
this is narrow and need not be further distinguished.
The sixth [consciousness] universally takes other [objects] as its objects.

Therefore, for the sake of brevity, the question asks: "If the aggregates (skandhas) include those that are untainted (anāsrava), why does it say only 'taking the five appropriated aggregates' (pañca-upādāna-skandha) as the object?
The answer is: This is stated in terms of the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) to mean that one takes the appropriated aggregates as the object.
Regarding "clinging" (upādāna):
according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises,
all four types of clinging are explained as being exclusively greed (*lobha*).
There are four kinds of clinging:
namely, clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a theory of self.
This is because the meaning of "clinging" consists in grasping the roots of dispute and grasping for future existence.
It continues, saying:
"Due to the causes of attachment to desire, bondage, and immersion in defilement,
these serve as the root of contention for all householders."
Because attachment to various views serves as the cause for bondage and defilement,
it constitutes the root of contention for those who have gone forth; therefore,
these four types of craving, when taken up as conditions, are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is said that craving is designated as "grasping" because its increase [is emphasized].

Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratā* states: "Although all afflictions are subsumed within the member of grasping (*upādāna*), craving is said to be the 'increase of craving' because its moistening power is predominant."
According to this, all afflictions are termed "grasping" (*upādāna*).
However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 89,
it is said that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are collectively termed "grasping."
Therefore, it says:
"One should know that herein, whether it be the grasped (grāhya), the grasper (grāhaka), or the purpose for which there is grasping—all such things are collectively termed 'grasping' (upādāna).
Question: What is that which is grasped?
Answer: Sensual desire, views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self are the objects of grasping (*upādāna*).
What is the grasper (*upādātṛ*)?
The four kinds of sensual craving (*kāmacchanda*) are the grasper.
For what purpose is there grasping?
It is for the sake of obtaining various desires and for the sake of enjoyment, and so forth; one should understand all such passages according to this principle.
If one takes "clinging" (*upādāna*) to refer specifically to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is so designated based on its predominance.
If it refers to that which grasps existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence, it encompasses all other defilements (*kleśa*).

If considered in terms of their mutual relationship, then the grasped object (*grāhya*), the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), and the purpose for which one grasps—namely, the apprehension of an object, the essence of grasping, and the cause of grasping—are all "clinging."
Each [explanation] relies on a specific meaning and they do not contradict one another;
various differing accounts should be reconciled according to this principle. Now, regarding what is called the "aggregates of appropriation" (upādānaskandha):

Whatever is grasped according to its respective conditions, and that which arises from grasping—namely, the grasped object (*grāhya*), the grasper (*grāhaka*), and that for which grasping is performed—all these are termed the aggregate of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
Question: Why is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) able to take both the bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*) as its objects?

I take only the aggregates (*skandha*) as my object; [whereas] the answer is that the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) can take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object and thus obtain the realms (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
I take only conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) as my object and cannot obtain the realms and bases universally.
Furthermore, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is mostly singular and permanent.
It does not take the elements (*dhātu*) or bases (*āyatana*) as its object;

because the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) is neither unitary nor permanent, it pervades the elements and bases. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this is stated by way of abbreviation based on the shadow [of the meaning].

This interpretation is correct. The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all taught for the purpose of refuting the self (*ātman*).
Therefore, one should know that the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) takes all three categories as its object.
These conditions, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, are discussed according to the Buddha-dharma.
Non-Buddhists do not establish the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*).
At the very first moment of seeing the Path, one is able to eliminate them.
There are four interpretations.
First, the distinction between the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). The path of seeing occurs at the beginning.
Second, the two truths are in mutual opposition.
The truth is present at the beginning;
the third and fourth paths are in opposition [to it].
It is not a stage of further progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*). Because it stands in opposition to the four uninterrupted paths and their liberations (*vimukti-mārga*),
and because it exists immediately after them, it is called the "first path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the phrase "worldly śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and so forth":
the term "and so forth" includes the four castes, beginning with the kṣatriyas.

Furthermore, it includes the *dhvaja* (translated here as "uncommon death"), the *pauṣkasa* (a jailer), the *caṇḍāla* (translated as "fierce" or "blazing"), the butcher, the *mleccha* (translated as "one who delights in filth"), the prostitute, the wine-seller, and the *kaṭhilla* (translated as "judge").
The treatise asks: "If there is no real self, how can there be such phenomena as recollection and recognition?
Ximing extensively cites eight arguments from the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* that explain the function of recollection. Now, I say this is not so.
Regarding the questions posed by the two or three types of non-Buddhists mentioned previously:
why is it necessary to separately describe the distinction of "manifestation" (*vyakti*) in order to make such a statement?
Within the exposition of our own doctrine, it is stated that recollection occurs only later due to the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
If the maturation-neutral [state] cannot itself perfuse [the seeds], one would subsequently be unable to remember.
Answer: It is not necessary for it to perfuse itself for one to be able to remember later. Why is this?
Although wholesome and unwholesome minds can indeed infuse seeds,
this does not preclude the existence of [a consciousness] that cannot remember.
Furthermore, how could the Buddha’s Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arise from recollection based on having previously seen an infusing agent during the causal stage?
If one were to claim that it is impossible for [the Buddha] to be perfumed because he cannot remember, this is incorrect;
for while in the causal state, all inferior untainted states and all tainted states have already been abandoned and do not perfume to form seeds.
After this point, by what means could one remember?
Therefore, we know that it is not the case that memory can only occur after being perfumed by its own kind;
rather, it is simply said to be "by means of perfuming."
It causes that [mind] to become increasingly luminous so that when it subsequently arises and manifests, one is able to remember.

This maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-citta*), being perfumed by wholesome and unwholesome minds, enables that recollection. Question: Since the three natures alternate with one another, how can the maturation-consciousness, perfumed by wholesome and unwholesome states, enable such recollection?
Question: How can one remember [an object] after the maturation (*vipāka*) of many thoughts has passed? Answer: Even if one cannot remember it, what fault is there?
For not all minds are capable of remembering; alternatively, that which is capable of remembering arises from seeds existing from the beginning.
Furthermore, as clarified in the *Suyao* (Essential Points) by the Dharma Master of Ximing, the *Yaoji* (Compendium of Essentials) states:
"In general discussion, there are two kinds of recollecting events:
first, the mind that is capable of recollecting."
Second, regarding the object remembered:
as for the mind capable of remembering, it is exclusively the sixth consciousness that can remember,
because it is associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Therefore, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The mental consciousness associated with mindfulness is able to remember;
although the objects previously experienced by various consciousnesses have ceased and lack substantiality."
The preceding moments of consciousness apprehend those objects and perfume them so as to form seeds that are not lost, and so forth.
Regarding the object being remembered, there are two meanings:
namely, remembering an object previously experienced.

Alternatively, one might argue that it is the mind capable of experiencing [the object] in the past that is now able to remember and so forth by virtue of the power of its own self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*). However, this explanation is said to be insufficient to exhaust the underlying principle.
Which vipāka-consciousnesses are incapable of perfuming seeds?
By what cause can one later recollect [them]?
Furthermore, not all objects of the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsajñāna) have been previously experienced.
In the state of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses are capable of recollecting the past;
it is not only the sixth consciousness. Therefore, [the previous] explanation was incomplete. Now, I shall provide the correct interpretation.
There are two categories of those capable of recollection:
first, Buddhas;
second, others.
There remains the state of having mastery and the state of not yet having mastery.
Regarding the state of not yet having mastery, there are two types:
first, the manifest;...
There are two kinds;
within the manifest [aspect], there are four.
First, the self-substance portion (svabhāva-bhāga).
Second, the power of perception;
third, the sixth mental consciousness associated with mindfulness;
fourth, the aggregate of mind and mental factors.
Based on the fact that a subsequent thought can recollect a preceding mind, it is specifically said that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the basis;
based on its limited scope regarding the specific objects recollected, it is specifically said that the power of perception (*saṃjñā*) is the basis;
and with respect to those who have not yet attained mastery, it refers only to the retrospective pursuit of the past.
This is a partial explanation referring specifically to the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with mindfulness.
To speak exhaustively according to principle,
all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with the sixth [consciousness] are collectively capable of recollecting.
If it refers to seeds, they are those aforementioned perfumable [factors].
Excluding only those seeds produced by the perfuming of the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) which serve as the cause for subsequent recollection,
or the seeds produced by the perfuming of the mental factors associated with mindfulness and perception within the sixth consciousness.
Regarding the ability to manifest birth and recollect [past lives], if one has attained mastery, there are further two categories:

namely, meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and the non-concentrated (*asamāhita*). Concentration is based on the impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*) [states], and upon the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*).
Only the sixth consciousness [is so]; however, if one relies on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), it extends to the seventh consciousness as well.

Since the seventh follows the lead of the sixth and shares the same objects of perception (*ālambana*) with it, there is no error in this. Furthermore, in the state of distraction (*vikṣipta*), it is already admitted that all sense faculties (*indriya*) are capable of mutual functioning.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses should also take the past as their object;

alternatively, although they may function interchangeably, they take only the present as their object. If one is in the state of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses are capable [of such functioning], but this occurs solely through the influence of causes.
Since there is no new seed in the fruit,
the treatise merely states that recollection and cognition arise through the power of perfuming;
it does not say that each [moment] perfumes itself and is able to recollect.
This explains the performance of karma and the reception of its fruits.
Within the eight consciousnesses of the Mahāyāna, they are distinguished by their presence or absence:
the first six possess both.
The seventh [category] possesses neither;
because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it does not perform karma,
and because it is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it does not receive the fruit.
The eighth, the experience of fruition, is neither capable of performing karma nor is it a ripening [cause],
because it is a ripened result and because it is of an indeterminate nature.
The five schools— the Vātsīputrīya, the Saṃmitīya, the Sūtrāntavāda, the Bhadrayānīya, and the Mahīśāsaka—
likewise maintain that the five consciousnesses cannot perform actions or receive their fruits.

The sixth [consciousness] is also capable [of performing action]. The Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools likewise maintain that all six consciousnesses are simultaneously capable of performing actions and receiving their fruits.
The Sarvāstivādins and others hold that the five consciousnesses receive the fruit but do not perform action, whereas the sixth [consciousness] is capable of both;
this explanation is based on oral tradition and has not been seen in the authentic scriptures.
This is recounted within the context of the Sāṃkhya tenets.
Question: Touch is taken as the wind-element (vāyu-mahābhūta), and the wind-element constitutes the tactile faculty (kāya-indriya).
Yet, while the tactile faculty perceives touch, it does not perceive the wind itself.
If that is so, what is the essence of contact? The answer is: it is composed of solidity, moisture, heat, hunger, and so forth, as well as the wind element;
it is distinct from the substance of wind itself, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others. Question: The skin does not perceive wind.
By what faculty is wind apprehended? Answer: By the faculty of mental equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
It is not necessarily apprehended by the faculty of touch.
This follows from the enumeration of the faculties as explained above.
This [text] must originally have been composed by the sage Kapila;
later, his various disciples divided into eighteen schools,
and the one who became a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) was the leader of one such school.
The *Saptati-śāstra* (Seventy Verses on Gold), also known as the *Vārṣagaṇya*, was composed by a certain individual among the followers of the Vārṣagaṇya school.
Why is this so? According to the oral tradition of the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, it is said: [text continues].
More than one thousand one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was a non-Buddhist teacher named Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja;
Piṇḍola is the name of a mountain.
"Vāsa" means "dwelling.
Because these non-Buddhists dwelt in this mountain, it was named after that fact.
There is a nāga king named Vīrasena.
A non-Buddhist practitioner, skilled in the Sāṃkhya treatises, resided within a great lake at the foot of this mountain.
Knowing that he wished to study under the dragon,
the dragon transformed his body into the form of a rishi and dwelt within a leaf-hut.
The non-Buddhist practitioners came to study.
Having completed their studies, they sought a debate to resolve matters of right and wrong.
They arrived at the kingdom of Yūṣa and struck the drum of King Śrīghoṣa to seek out a formal discussion.
Having composed the treatise because of the gold,
he intended to go to his appointed destination; while traveling to the mountain retreat,
he summoned a yakṣī by the power of reciting mantras.
It was named Gahvara. He made a request of it, saying:
"After my death, may my body transform into stone and never decay."
The goddess granted her request.
After she sacrificed her life within the stone cave, her body transformed into rock.
For what reason did she make this vow?
The former dragon king, wishing to destroy the doctrines of these Sāṃkhya teachers,
requested from the dragon king that his own body be destroyed only when the Dharma was extinguished.
The dragon king thought to himself:
"How could this body endure for long?
Thinking thus, he immediately granted her request;
therefore, he has now transformed his body into stone so that it may endure.
For this reason, the stream of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has continued down to the present day.
Later, the Bodhisattva Dignāga refuted its tenets and composed a treatise on inference (*anumāna*) upon this stone;
though he broke into a sweat and cried out, he was unable to save it.
Consequently, the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) composed by Dignāga flourished throughout the four quarters, its fame resounding across the five regions;
it was indeed for this reason.
Some claim that the Ṛṣi Kapila composed the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) and remained in the form of a stone within the Āmalaka forest; this appears to be an error.
However, tradition states that one thousand and one hundred years later, this non-Buddhist (tīrthika) appeared and composed the *Saptatiśāstra* (Seventy Treatise).
When Vasubandhu appeared, the non-Buddhists had already been extinguished;
it is said that Vasubandhu also appeared one thousand years later,
but this tradition seems to be erroneous.
Why is this? The preface to the *Commentary on the Distinction Between the Middle and the Extremes* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha was produced nine hundred years ago;
the non-Buddhists likewise existed nine hundred years prior [to that].
If this were not so, how could that treatise be explained? Some say that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"In ancient times there was a seer named Jātiśroṇa;
that seer composed a treatise named *Samīkṣā*."
This is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
It extensively elucidates the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
According to this, contemplation is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
Its name is the same as that of the Sāṃkhya [system].
Since "saṃkhyā" means wisdom (*prajñā*),
it refers to this very treatise.
As for the seer named Jātiśroṇa,
this is merely a phonetic corruption;
he is none other than the seer Kapila.
Commentary:
Furthermore, the three [qualities] are the particulars, while the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are the universals.
Below, the refutation of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) is presented in five sections.
As categorized in the commentary:
first, the refutation by analogy with the characteristics of the essence;
second, the refutation that the time of transformation is like the original.
3. Refutation by the loss of the three natures according to their characteristics;
4. Refutation by the principle that the general and specific characteristics should not be limited to one or three;
5. Refutation by each possessing the three natures. In the first part of the fifth section, the thesis is restated.
Next is the refutation.
This refutation further consists of five parts.
First, the general refutation corresponding to the three [previous] refutations.
1. Two or three things would not differ from the refutation.
2. Three [things] would possess the capacity to establish the refutation. 3. The essence [of the subject] would consequently not be one. 4. The refutation [itself] would be non-unitary.
Fifth is the refutation through multiple contradictions, which corresponds respectively to the sequential divisions of the commentary.
The treatise states: "Since there are already three characteristics, how can they be seen as one?"
In our own Mahāyāna school, the primary matter and the derived matter produced from it occupy the same location;
yet their essence and characteristics must be distinct.
How, then, can they be seen as one?
Furthermore, just as multiple cognitions arise with respect to a single object and undergo simultaneous transformation, one should likewise perceive diversity.
Why, then, does one perceive it as a single [object]? Answer: It is not the same as that case.
Because they are not real,
their own nature is empty and insubstantial;
because they are summoned by common karma.
Therefore, they appear as one.

As for the question in the treatise: "Should it not follow that a single faculty could perceive all objects, since [the faculties] are composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)?"—in the Buddha-dharma, the five faculties are all produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and their essence consists of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*).
Question: Why do the various sense organs not apprehend all objects? Answer: Each arises from its own specific seed, and the four great elements (mahābhūta) are composed of coarse matter.
This differs from those [objects], which are all composed of the three qualities (triguṇa).
In the *Vyākhyā* [commentary] on the Vaiśeṣika tenets, it is stated: "The earth is manifested by means of its qualities."
It serves merely as the basis for color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility;
it is by means of those qualities that depend upon it that the substance of this "earth" is manifested.
If these qualities were lacking, it would not be designated as "earth."
The remaining elements, such as water and fire, should be understood accordingly.
Because this self (*ātman*) serves as the causal condition for the conjunction of the nine factors— such as cognition, pleasure, and pain— once they have conjoined,
it gives rise to the characteristic of consciousness, which is termed the "self."
Furthermore, the self (*puruṣa*) is manifested by means of those characteristics such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
This is the intended meaning. Question: Why is it that the mind (*manas*) is defined as the cause for the non-conjunction of the nine qualities, such as cognition (*buddhi*), and so forth?
Is it that his intention is actually not the mental faculty (manas-indriya)? If it were the mental faculty, [how could this be so]?
The arising of the mind depends upon it;

how can one say that it is not a cause and condition for conjunction? The explanation says: because the intention regards the nine virtues as remote, it cannot act as a cause and condition for their conjunction;
therefore, it is called a "cause and condition of non-conjunction."
It is not that those nine qualities are combined and yet discordant.
Regarding "that which is apprehended by the eye is based on one thing, namely name-and-form (nāmarūpa)":
a single atom of form is based on the earth element and so forth.
It is called "form" (rūpa) because it is apprehended by the eye;
the remaining [objects] are to be understood accordingly.
This is because those five sense faculties are themselves the five great elements (mahābhūta).
The color of an atom (paramāṇu) depends on the great elements (mahābhūta) of its respective sense-base;
when it is apprehended by the eye,
it is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) based on that single designation.
Regarding the statement that "a single atom exists only as a result upon two atoms":
because when those two parent atoms combine, this atomic measure exists upon the resulting atom;
thus, it serves as the basis for perceiving the most subtle form.
That which does not unite with the parents is so because it is neither a sense faculty (*indriya*) nor an object (*viṣaya*); thus,
there is neither union nor separation.
One takes only the initial conjunction as "conjunction" and the initial separation as "separation";
thereafter, they are no longer so.
Regarding that which is the object of dependence for distant cognition and constitutes its nature:

it is called "that" because the grasping mind takes it as its object from a distance. As for the phrase "conjunction": *Note: The term "andha-jñāna" (blind cognition) refers here to a cognition that arises in dependence on an external object located at a distance, such as the perception of a mirage or a distant mountain.*
It causes that earth and so forth to be conjoined with qualities,
yet remains distinct from that self;
the self merely causes those nine qualities— such as cognition, pleasure, and pain— to be conjoined.
"Taking" refers to first joining and subsequently separating, discussed in terms of above and below;
"moving" refers specifically to [the body] remaining on the ground and so forth.
Question: Why are visual consciousness and the others not established?
Answer: They are precisely [the functions of] discernment (*vitarka*) and so forth.
Many other calculations of non-Buddhists are also based on this principle.
Within the various classifications of the gates,
regarding the distinction between the many and the one: there are four categories of the many and one category of the one.
Because "I" and the mind depend upon a single person, they are designated as one;
however, if considered in relation to many persons, they are multiple.
Space, time, and direction are common to all.
There is no plurality of entities that is designated as "one.
As for the statement that fragrance exists only in earth because it is explained according to the perspective of causes and conditions,
this is because it is analyzed within the section on cause and effect in that root treatise.
Heaviness is generally impermanent.
If that is so, how can it be perceived solely by direct perception?
It is because only the subtle essence of the parents is permanent, and thus not perceptible.
Answer: There is no textual explanation for this in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

By inferring from the meaning, it is unobjectionable to consider that [the cognition] applies to both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, since fragrance is exclusively impermanent, how could it not be subsumed under perception?
Answer: Although fragrance is impermanent, it does not cease [to exist] but merely resides upon the flower;
therefore, it is generally not manifest.
Regarding the statement in the exposition of the [opponent's] views that "many [factors] substantially exist":
I shall now further assist in the explanation.
Within the context of the "real entity" (*vastu*), the army, forest, and so forth are cited as they are explained in the treatises;
these serve as concordant examples (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of refuting their substantial existence.
These few [points] are provisional;
since the remainder is mostly real, the structural outline follows the commentary. Now, to assist [the reader], one section is divided into two parts.
First, it refutes [the notion of] substantial existence;

by stating "it illuminates that such substantiality and so forth are not objects apart from consciousness," it subsequently refutes [the claim that they are] obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Based on the enumeration of their tenets, two sections have been established. The treatise states:

"Furthermore, those elements they grasp—earth, water, fire, and wind—should not be subsumed under the category of 'substantial entities possessing resistance,' because they are touched by the body-faculty," and so forth.
The *Yaoji* states:
Some say that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth, water, fire, and wind belonging to parents are not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whereas the atoms of the offspring and those above them are obtained through direct perception.
The *Lokāyata-bhaṅga* and the *Vaiśeṣika-bhaṅga* state:
"Since the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is sufficient to constitute the sense faculties and their objects, what need is there for a 'result' (*phala*)?
Thus, it should be understood accordingly.
Some explain that the five phrases beginning with "substance" (*dravya*) are the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whereas their combination is not.
Therefore, the following refutation states:
Since even those things such as "substance" (dravya) that they admit are obtained through direct perception (pratyakṣa) are not truly existent when subjected to logical analysis,
how much less so their own admitted category of "inherence" (saṃyoga), which is not obtained through direct perception?
And thus they can truly exist.
From this it is proven that the atoms of the parents are also apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). There is an interpretation which says:
Now, it is said that the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) produced from two subtle atoms is likewise not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states that it is only when a [subtle atom] is produced from three subtle atoms that it becomes coarse enough to be perceived through conjunction.
The following explains the coarse material dimension and its conjunction with qualities;
for this reason, it is apprehended by the material sense faculties. The *Ji* states:
"Now, I maintain that the aforementioned interpretation is correct."
That is to say, in that school it is not asserted that only what is apprehended by the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) constitutes the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There are objects of direct perception that are not necessarily apprehended by the material sense-faculties;
and so on, up to where it says:
Some say that within the context of refuting the Lokāyata,
since many causes consist of the conjunction of atoms, it should suffice for the sense-faculties and their objects to be subtle;
what need is there for a "result" (the composite whole)?
From this it is proven that from the *putu* (*puti*) upward is the objective domain of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). That which is not [of this level],
such as the *bāmu* (*bābǔ*), refutes being the objective domain of the material sense-faculties.

To state that direct perception (pratyakṣa) has not yet been discussed and to cite the fact that it does not take non-material sensory objects as its domain as proof that it is not attained through direct perception is far too tenuous in terms of reasoning.
Now, to examine this meaning in detail:
it is said that some have not yet realized the ultimate principle.
Why is this? As the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states:

That is to say, when there is contact between the actual object, such as form, and the sense faculties, etc., and there arises a cognition of the characteristic of the object, this is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since it has been stated that "when there is contact between the sense faculties, etc., and there arises a cognition of the characteristic of the object, this is called direct perception," [the definition is established].
They maintain that only when the subtle atom (paramāṇu) has already combined with its object is it called direct perception (pratyakṣa); this is their doctrinal position.
The following passage cites [the opponent's view] to refute the defense offered by the Lokāyatas and others.
It is said that because an effect is composed of many parts, it becomes coarse;
since many atoms (paramāṇu) must combine to form a cause, they should not be subtle enough to constitute the objects of the sense faculties.
Rather, it is intended that an effect formed by the combination of many [atoms] becomes coarse and thus constitutes the object of the material sense faculties.
Therefore, taking this as proof, [the state] from the subtle (*sūkṣma*) upward is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
On what basis is it a remote [object],
such that you falsely claim it to be an error?
If the explanation based on existence were correct,
the five propositions would be established as mutually acknowledged in the present; however,
on what textual authority is it said that the subtle [self] within parents is an object of one's own direct perception?
In the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*, it is stated that only the quality of cognition (*buddhi-guṇa*) constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is based on perception and inference.
Furthermore, it says that when the sense organs and other factors come together, the arising of a cognition is termed "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*);
it does not state that the self (*ātman*) is the essence of direct perception.
Furthermore, there is no scriptural statement that the atoms of the parents or the self are apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If one relies on the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), there is an interpretation that does not contradict [this];
however, if discussed in detail, it is better to say that they do exist.
Regarding the argument that their asserted existence of "reaching" (*prāpti*), "as-it-is-ness" (*yathārthatva*), "virtue" (*guṇa*), and so forth,

both the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Shuyao* (Essentials of the Pivot) state that these are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by contradiction with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viruddha-hetu*) of phenomena.

Regarding the argument that "our own position possesses an intrinsic nature because it is certainly distinct from the category of the real and is admitted not to be non-existent, like qualities, actions, and so forth"—
this proof is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
In reality, this is a dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*), because it is admitted that [the reason] does not apply to what is causeless among real entities (*vastu*).
Furthermore, there are other faults;
these may be understood by applying the same principle of analysis.
Now, let us first demonstrate that your position is internally contradictory.
You claim that "you possess an intrinsic nature," yet apart from the actual referent (*vastu*), there is no separate intrinsic nature.
Because it is admitted that [the property] is not non-existent,
just like the category of "real entities" (*dravya-pada*). Within this formal argument (*pramāṇa*), although there is an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy due to others,
categories such as "qualities" (*guṇa-pada*) and "actions" (*karma-pada*) are admitted by others to be not non-existent.
Since it is not commonly accepted by both parties that [the reason] functions based on that [subject], it is not an "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) fallacy.
Furthermore, when refuting another, it may also be treated as a fault of being inconclusive with respect to that other party;
therefore, the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) judges that this is subsumed solely under the fallacy of contradicting inference (*anumāna-viruddha*).
If one follows the judgment of the *Śāstra* (Commentary), it states:
"Apart from the eight categories such as 'substance' (*dravya*), there is no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

thus, there is no 'indefinite' (*anaikāntika*) [reason]. The *Yāoyí* (Essential Compendium) says: "According to the counter-argument (*pratikūla-pramāṇa*), it is said that 'existence' (*sattā*) exists."
Apart from the real, there is no separate intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because it is admitted not to be non-existent;
this is just like the category of the real.
This would constitute a contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*). This essential point has already been adjudicated by [the author] himself.

The *Yāojí* (Essential Compendium) raises an objection, stating: "Since the example is employed separately, how can it be contradictory? It is the same as the aforementioned 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*) fallacy. This argument is also incorrect.
What is meant by "even if a separate example is provided, it is still contradictory"? For instance, in the *Nyāyapraveśa*,
outside of the category of the "contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic" (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*),
one might establish that sound is eternal.
"Because it is a product,
like space. [The opponent] states the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) as follows:
Sound is impermanent because it is produced,
just like a jar and other such things.
This reason employs the same example as before;
now, this logical reason (*hetu*) also employs the same [reason] as before, with only the similar example (*sapakṣa*) being modified,
in accordance with the *Hetuprakaraṇa* (Logic).
To ask how it is contradictory for the cloud to be used as a distinct metaphor is to raise a groundless objection;
such a person is unskilled in *hetuvidyā* (logic).
The *Śāstra* says:
"If one departs from reality and so forth, it is like that which is ultimately non-existent.
The *Shuyao* says:
This is the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*). Furthermore, it is said:
"Now, even if one employs a non-existent thing as an example, it still constitutes a definitive contradiction (*viruddha*), just as stated in the treatise."
Regarding the statement that if one departs from existent phenomena (bhāva), there is a separate nature of non-existence (abhāva),
the *Shuyao* states:
"The third and fourth [positions] both contradict inference (*anumāna*)."
As stated in the commentary (*śū*),
the *Yāoji* says: Some say that the measure (*pramāṇa*) is as follows.
Regarding your tenth category, "non-existence beyond existence," you should establish it as a distinct nature.
The reason is that, apart from the six categories such as "great existence" (mahāsattā), the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory.
Regarding "as it is," "virtue," and "action":

in order to exclude indeterminate causes, the six phrases beginning with "except for the great existence" (*mahāsattā*) are set forth. One interpretation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) states that the five kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*) should have their own distinct ontological categories (*dharmasvabhāva*).
Because they are subsumed under either existence or non-existence;
for instance, reality (*tattva*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. Furthermore, according to your own statement, reality and the others should have no distinct nature (*bhinnasvabhāva*).
Because it is subsumed under either existence or non-existence within the pair of these two;

just as with absolute non-existence, the *Yaoji* merely cites the two schools [of thought] without knowing their respective strengths and weaknesses. Based on the explanation of existence, the aforementioned formal argument (*pramāṇa*) incurs the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the five kinds of non-entities (*abhāva*), they should have a nature distinct from the three categories such as "as-it-is" (*tathatā*) and so forth;
or alternatively, they should not have a nature distinct from the three categories such as "great existence" (*mahāsattā*) and so forth. The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) further states:

Some say that both [the existent and the non-existent] lack an intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), yet this does not mean that the absence of intrinsic nature itself is non-existent; nor is there a "non-existence" established without a basis.
Furthermore, the substance of an existent phenomenon is not non-existent.
Why is it necessary to establish "existence" as a separate category?
If they offer this defense:
"Although a phenomenon is not non-existent, it does not exist of itself; therefore, 'existence' must exist."

Furthermore, there should be no phenomenon that is not non-existent; apart from non-existence, one cannot establish "existence" as something separate. This is what they mean by looking at them in relation to one another.
My current interpretation is this:
the essence of an existent phenomenon is not non-existent.
Because existence exists, there is the nature of existence;
a non-existent entity is not existent. Because non-existence does not exist, there is no nature of non-existence.
Alternatively,
the opponent may say:
existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive.
There is no phenomenon that lacks the nature of existence;
existence and non-existence are mutually relative.
There is a phenomenon that possesses the nature of existence.
This response is always distinct [from the objection];
how, then, could it refute the opponent?
Therefore, in this treatise, we employ only formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute them.
It is not necessary that they must both [be present]; I now maintain that even if they were both present, one would still be able to refute the other.
For instance, the *Saṃyukta-vyākhyā* cannot avoid this fault. Why?
If it is said that there is no essence of dharmas and that they are not existent—
If there were no cause, there would be no nature of non-existence;
yet it would follow that the essence of phenomena exists inherently.
If there were existence, there would be no nature of existence.
That which has the nature of an existent exists by itself;
because it exists, its existence-nature is established.
That which has the nature of a non-existent is non-existent.
To establish non-existence without cause is to fall into the error of having existence within opposition;
there can be no relative correspondence between them.
An existent phenomenon establishes the nature of existence;
non-existence cannot do so because it is contradictory.
A non-existent phenomenon establishes the nature of non-existence.
It is constantly not free from faults.
The treatise says:
"Let it not be that this [entity] is also not of the nature of real qualities and activities."

This refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the entity under discussion. The phrase "not having the nature of substance, quality,
or activity" intends to say:
It is not real; its qualities, etc., are distinct from it,
because they are different from the real, etc.,
just like qualities and actions.
Because the distinctions of virtue and karma are not the same as the nature of identity and difference.
The treatise says:
"Furthermore, regarding the wisdom that takes reality as its object," and so forth.
It destroys the wisdom that takes [the object] as its cognitive support.
The Commentary provides two interpretations, as it arises through a provisional combination.
According to the first interpretation, it takes many dharmas as its cognitive support.
Later, when liberating wisdom arises, it relies upon many conditions;
it does not obstruct the subjective cognition from taking those—whether one or many—as its objects.
If one follows the first interpretation:
It merely refutes the collective condition (*sāmānyālambana*) but does not refute the individual conditions (*viśeṣālambana*);
the subsequent explanation refutes both.
Although the objects of perception may be either singular or manifold, [the refutation applies].
The wisdom that takes [an object] as its cognitive support must depend on multiple conditions; thus, it is said to arise through provisional conjunction (*prajñapti-saṃghāta*).
The *Yào jí* states: "Now, I say that the latter interpretation of the first master is also not definitive.

Because the wisdom of the realization of the actual object is like the real, while the wisdom of their conjunction arises through provisional conjunction, it is the wisdom of the cognition of the real."

If it is argued that [the cognition] of qualities, actions, and commonality or difference is not a cognition of reality because it arises from a conceptual synthesis, we shall now examine this statement to show that it falsely attributes a fault to our position. Why?
Because if one considers it in terms of a general synthesis (*sāmānyālambana*), [it is indeed so].
If "conditioned by existence" (*bhava-pratyaya*) is a synthesis, it is likewise a real entity (*vastu*).
Thus, within the dharma itself, that which is precisely being refuted does not entail the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
If one refutes the separate conditions as being a synthesis conditioned by existence, [the same applies].
Although it arises through a provisional combination and thus does not take a real entity as its object, there is no lack of definiteness.
Regarding the two explanations: the former refers to the fact that cognition can only arise when there are multiple objects, which is termed "arising through a provisional combination."
Later, when many conditions and cognitions come together, it is only then that the name "arising" can be applied; this is called "arising through provisional conjunction.
This is not intended to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). The Commentary states:
Although visual consciousness and the others arise through a provisional combination even when taking form and so forth as their objects,
there is no fault of indeterminacy because they do not take [the category of] "real" and so forth as their objects. Some say:
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with [your own position]: cognition conditioned by form and so forth would not be "cognition of form," as it arises from a conventional combination.
Therefore, regarding the cognition of sound and so forth, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"This is not a fault.
That is to say, internally one refutes the external [view] that the four great elements and their derived matter, such as color, are subsumed under [the categories of] substance and quality."
Therefore, it does not contradict the phenomena of form and so forth, which are subsumed within the aggregates and other categories.
If an opponent were to employ such an inference to refute [this position],
they would incur faults such as contradicting worldly convention, direct perception, and their own scriptures.
Therefore, it cannot be established. Now, we say this is not so.
Even if one maintains that [the object] is perceived apart from the aggregates such as consciousness, it is likewise refuted by this same argument.
The intent of this treatise is merely to refute the existence of dharmas as real entities apart from consciousness.
If an external objection states that cognition which takes as its object form (*rūpa*) and so forth, being separated from consciousness, should not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

then one commits the fallacy of contradiction (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*). If, however, one simply says that cognition taking form and so forth as its object [is direct perception], [the objection does not apply].
It is not subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding form and so forth;
furthermore, it possesses partial correspondence as well as internal contradictions.
If it were established as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would not incur the aforementioned faults of the previous [means].
The treatise says:
"If a phenomenon is capable of producing [something], it must necessarily be impermanent.
Question: If one grants that other phenomena can serve as productive causes, [what follows?]
This contradicts their own tenets because they maintain that there is a single cause.
Since there is no other capacity to produce [the effect], the positive example (*sapakṣa*) is lacking. How can that which produces be impermanent? Answer: The deity is the proximate productive cause.
The others are auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), and therefore they can serve as metaphors. If that is so, how can they function as causes?

Because there is a distinction between the two types: causal origination (*hetu-samutpāda*) and conditional origination (*pratyaya-samutpāda*). Answer: This accords with the principles of *hetuvidyā* (logic).
The reason should not be differentiated,
just like the property of being produced;
for both this reason and the conditions are capable of producing [the effect].
The Ximing commentary states:
"Only a single eternal cause can produce all phenomena;
there is no other eternal thing capable of acting as a cause to produce them."
This is called the theory of a single cause.
It holds that what is impermanent does not obstruct the production of various phenomena,
just as the Vaiśeṣika masters accept the six categories of substance.

It does not preclude the possibility that both interpretations regarding the "forest of the central army" (*madhyama-senā-vana*) and so forth incur the fault of contradicting the text, because one maintains [the position] based on a single cause.
In the subsequent discussion of alternative views, it says: "it depends upon desire or conditions."

The objection states: "If [a thing] can only arise when dependent upon desire or conditions, this contradicts the doctrine of a single cause. If others admit that there are other conditions capable of producing [the effect] and that there is a cause for impermanence, how could such an objection be made?"

In this context, only those phenomena commonly accepted by the world as being capable of producing [effects] are used as the concordant examples (*sapakṣa*). Furthermore, it is explained that the fundamental tenet [of the opponent] holds that the essence of Īśvara is a single, eternal entity capable of producing all phenomena.
That which can produce [an effect] only when not assisted by other factors is called a "sole cause" (*ekahetu*).
Furthermore, that which does not obstruct other factors can also function as a cause.
Now, the author of the treatise raises an objection:
Since its essence is eternal and omnipresent, it should be able to produce all phenomena at all times.
Consequently, they further argue that Īśvara requires other factors— such as desire or conditions— in order to be able to produce effects.
The Master of the Treatise says:
If that were so, it would contradict the original [position] that a single, eternal cause is still capable of producing effects;
because it depends upon desire and conditions, it contradicts the theory of a single cause.
The *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"If it possesses spatial divisions, it must be provisional and not real;
if it lacks spatial divisions, it would be like the mind and mental factors."
According to their fundamental theory,
there are only the four great elements, yet they also claim these produce the mind.
However, as with the mind and mental factors, there is no similar example [to illustrate this].
The outsider says: "The four great elements that constitute the pure and subtle mind are unimpeded;
it is because they constitute coarse and large matter that there is obstruction.
The second says: "Although it consists solely of derived matter..."
According to reason, it is also appropriate that there be both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*),
as the Sāṃkhya masters maintain.
Thirdly, regarding the Vaiśeṣika school, the presence of mind and mental factors is cited as a concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
The Commentary states:

"In this case, one should simply say that it is like two atoms [producing] a third atom; for the cause is not an atom, but rather the magnitude of the third sub-atom (putra-aṇu) as the effect is equal to the cause.
This meaning holds that the magnitude of the third sub-atom as the effect is equal to the cause.
However, this is coarse matter and not ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*).
First, within the refutation of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), matter is refuted as an aggregate;
furthermore, within that aggregate of matter, there are three [types].
First, resistance through obstruction;
second, resistance through the object-field;
third, resistance through the focal object. Regarding "resistance through obstruction":

This refers to the mutual obstruction between the five sense faculties and the five sense objects. Regarding "obstruction by way of objective domain" (*viṣayapratighāta*), it refers to the twelve elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of the element of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The twelve elements are the seven consciousness elements and the five sense-faculty elements.

Because every portion of the *dharmadhātu* possesses the capacity to grasp an object, yet it is constrained by the aspect of the object such that the sense faculties and the mind do not turn toward anything else; therefore, it is called "resistance regarding the objective field" (*viṣayapratighata*). As for what is called "resistance regarding the focal object" (*ālambanapratighata*):
This refers to the seven consciousness elements and a portion of the dharma element.
As for "object" (ālambana):
these mental factors are called objects because they are capable of having an object.

Resistance by way of the object refers to the constraining of the mind to that object so that it does not turn elsewhere; this is called resistance with respect to the focal object (*ālambana-pratighāta*). Question: What is the difference between the two types of resistance, namely *ālambana* (focal object) and *viṣaya* (objective sphere)? Answer: With respect to the focal object (*ālambana*), it pertains to the essential nature of the mind and its associates as being capable of cognizing and deeply discerning the object.
It is that which can be clearly distinguished within an object.
As the *Śāstra* states:
"The mind and mental factors grasp that [object] and arise in relation to it; because it exists in relation to the mind and so forth, it is called the 'object-condition' (*ālambana*)."
Regarding the sensory bases (āyatana) that possess resistance, as well as the faculties (indriya):
the faculties are merely able to illuminate [the object] but cannot apprehend its specific modes of activity (ākāra), and thus their functioning is shallow.
This is because the faculty’s grasping of the object arises simultaneously with consciousness.
One does not grasp [the object] through deep penetration, but rather grasps the functional capacity to illuminate the object.
Because it illuminates in the same manner as the sense organ, the *Śāstra* states:
"If this [consciousness] possesses the functional capacity for that phenomenon..."
That is precisely what is stated to be the objective sphere (*gocara*) of this dharma;
thus, the two are distinct.
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* provides a complete explanation [of this].

One should further examine the texts to determine this definitively. Question: What is the distinction between the "object-field" (viṣaya) and the "obstructive" (pratigha), which occur simultaneously? Answer: That which possesses the characteristics of mutual opposition and spatial limitation is called "obstructive resistance" (sapratigha).
When the sense faculties grasp their objects, they are obstructed and do not function toward others.

This obstruction does not prevent other things from arising; therefore, it is not called "obstruction by way of an object" (*viṣayāvaraṇa-pratighāta*). Question: In the Sarvāstivāda school, is there "obstruction by way of resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*) within the form included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*)? Answer: No.
Why is this? Because unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is not composed of atoms;
rather, it is produced solely by the four great elements acting at a distance.
Furthermore, for example, at the time of currently performing the ritual for receiving the precepts,
although there is no unmanifest [matter],
the four great elements have already been suspendedly produced as that future unmanifest matter.
Because it is neither identical to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) nor to the atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is not "resistant form" (*sapratigha-rūpa*).

Question: What is the difference between the new and old Sarvāstivāda schools regarding how atoms constitute coarse matter? Answer: First, the old Sarvāstivāda holds that coarse matter is constituted by seven atoms.
Because they are closely proximate, they appear as a single characteristic;
however, in reality, each of the seven atoms constitutes a coarse form individually, and it is not said that they depend upon one another.
According to the newer Sarvāstivādins, these seven atoms aggregate together.
They are mutually proximate and support one another, each contributing its own force to constitute their respective gross characteristics (*mahābhūta*).
It is not by the mere conjunction of similar characteristics that they first become gross.
This is also like the case of colors such as long and short.
There is the characteristic of an extremely subtle atom that is long,
and there is the characteristic of an extremely subtle atom that is short; however, within this school, a short color can exist within a long color,
unlike the case with the dharmas of lightness and heaviness.
What is heavy must necessarily lack lightness; what is light must necessarily lack heaviness.
One does not establish lightness and heaviness by means of mutual comparison.
It is simply said that what cannot be weighed is called "light," while objects that can be weighed are termed "heavy. Therefore,
in this context, we shall first refute the Sautrāntika masters and the *savipākavarṇa* (manifest form) of the Sarvāstivādins.

First, the means of establishment are refuted, followed by the object of establishment. Now, there is a thesis which claims that seven ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one *niravayava-rūpa* (a unitary material form).
According to this view, light does not penetrate them; rather, they are situated at a distance from one another equal to one atom.
When both the object and the subject are real,
the five consciousnesses are obtained starting from the coarse form;
if each individual atom is the object, it is obtained only by the mental consciousness.
It is not the object of the five consciousnesses.
Regarding the objects of the five consciousnesses, the Sautrāntika school’s position is the same as that of the Vaibhāṣika school:
they maintain that the seven atoms (*paramāṇu*) which constitute the manifest form are real entities.
The derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) is conventional. Question: Within which of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are these two categories—the seven subtle particles—subsumed?
Answer: If one says they are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are subsumed under the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
However, according to the present school (the Sarvāstivāda), the subtle is subsumed within the coarse; thus, they are collectively gathered into the base of form (*rūpāyatana*).

If the Sautrāntika masters maintain that [the elements] are subsumed under the real and their substance is subsumed under the conventional, and that their essence is also subsumed under the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana), then a question arises:
since it is admitted that the four great elements (mahābhūta) produce atoms (paramāṇu), there must already be four atoms within a single atom.
If one follows the principle that each of the seven atoms has its own four [elements], totaling twenty-eight, why is it said that there are only "seven gaṇas"?
Furthermore, including the four great elements, there would be one hundred and forty. Answer: To speak according to the actual reality, there are logically twenty-eight.

However, these are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and are not apprehended by the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*). Since we are now taking up only the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses,
there is no logical error in stating that each consists of seven atoms (*paramāṇu*), even if one does not mention the principle of their being produced [by other elements].

If one says that the conventional atom (*saṃvṛti-paramāṇu*) can establish both the producer and the produced, then both are common to being real and conventional. Furthermore, regarding whether the atom is conventional or real, there is a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhāga*):
first, the coarse is conventional while the subtle is real.
According to the Sautrāntika masters,
the two [types of atoms] are coarse and real, while the subtle is conventional; in the Mahāyāna, even the atom (paramāṇu) is conventional.
That which is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is established as a conceptual construct; thus,
three are coarse and fine, while all are real.
The Sarvāstivādins [hold that] both the coarse and the subtle are conventionally designated (*prajñapti*).
There is also one school that asserts they are conventionally designated, and so forth; furthermore, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
One [school] holds that both the coarse and the subtle are conventional;
one is the Ekavyāvahārika school,
and the other is the Sarvāstivāda school.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that both [types of atoms] are conventional designations, as well as supramundane [phenomena].

Both types of non-entities are the ultimate truth according to Bhāviveka. Furthermore, regarding the subtle aggregate (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*), the treatise says, following a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*:
"In the realm of desire, the subtle aggregate is without sound."
The rootless [consciousness] consists of eight bases;
that with the body-root consists of nine bases;
and the remaining roots consist of ten bases.
If this mind possesses the body faculty, it necessarily consists of nine entities;
with any one of the remaining four [faculties], it becomes ten entities.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
If one speaks of eight, nine, ten, and so forth based on their essential nature (*tattva*), it would be too few;
if one speaks of eight, nine, ten, and so forth based on their locations (*sthāna*), it would be too many. The answer is: there is no fault.
Regarding what is called "the thing" (*vastu*): one part is explained in terms of its substance (*dravya*), namely the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its basis;
another part is explained in terms of its location (*sthāna*).
That is to say, it refers to the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) which depends [upon them]. Furthermore, an objection is raised:

"If that were so, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would become multiple entities, because each type of derived matter depends upon its own distinct set of four primary elements. The response is: "It should be understood that here the term 'dependence' is stated in terms of their generic categories (*jāti*)."
Because there is no distinction among the various types of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding their function, the Sarvāstivādins ask in the *Vibhāṣā*: "Are past dharmas many?"
Are future phenomena more numerous?
One master says that past phenomena are more numerous,
because they have no beginning.
First, because they have flowed into the past;
second, because future dharmas are numerous,
for the future is inexhaustible.
Third, they are similar in their explanations.
The Buddha said that because dharmas have no coming or going,
how can there be the three periods of time?
By means of this single dharma:
that which is currently functioning is called the present;
that which has already functioned is called the past.
"That which has not yet performed its activity is called 'future,'" the Abhidharmakośa masters refute [this view], saying:
"It would entail the fallacy of the three time periods being intermingled,
because you define the present as that which performs its activity."
Since the arising function and the luminosity of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) both possess utility in the future,
and since the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) possesses its utility only when it has fallen into the past,
they would all necessarily be present.
"Because there is activity. The *Nyāya* rescues [the position] by saying:
"The present self is activity; the past and future are potentialities (*śakti*)."
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* composed by Vasubandhu further refutes [this], saying:
"What distinction is there between your 'activity' (*kāritra*) and 'efficacy' (*sāmarthya*)?
A treatise must necessarily possess distinctions of the upper, lower, and the four cardinal directions."
According to the principles of their own fundamental school, that [atom] has no spatial dimensions;
yet now, by means of logical inference, it is forced to have spatial dimensions,
with the six directions— above, below, and the four cardinal points— each corresponding to one another.
If they lacked spatial dimensions, they would necessarily interpenetrate one another;
therefore, in the *Vibhāṣā*, the Venerable Mahādeva stated that atoms lack spatial dimensions yet do not reach one another.
"Flowing until they reach the present" means becoming proximate;
that is, these atoms were each separated from one another in the future world,
but only upon flowing into the present world do they finally become proximate.
Because there is no interval between the atoms that are separated [by space], it is called "reaching" (*prāpti*);
it is not called "reaching" because of physical contact.
The Bodhisattva Vasumitra does not accept that explanation, stating: [as follows].
If that were the case, the preceding atom would have to remain until the subsequent moment.
According to their own tenet, an atom remains for only a single kṣaṇa before entering the past.
If it is only when it reaches the present that it is said to "arrive" and thus become proximate, [then this definition is untenable].
That is to say, it consists of two moments;
this falling-away subtle flow reaches the present world,
for it is only by abiding in the present that it becomes proximate.
Vasumitra explains:
when various atoms exist simultaneously in the present,
their mutual proximity such that there is no intervening space between them is termed "contact" (prāpti).
In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, Vasubandhu refutes this, asking:
"By what means can there be an obstruction that creates an interval between them?
Furthermore, these spatial dimensions are analyzed through a fourfold logical permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, according to the Sautrāntika school, substantial atoms possess spatial dimensions;
second, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, substantial atoms lack spatial dimensions;
third, according to the Mahāyāna school, conventional atoms both possess and lack spatial dimensions.
Regarding that which illuminates:
because there are no atoms within the great provisional form, it is said to have no spatial divisions (*digbhāga*).
However, if one analyzes the coarse through provisional means down to the ultimate atom, one may say that it possesses spatial divisions.
Spatial dimensions are of two kinds: first,
the dimension of a single direction,
which is a portion of that great form.
It is not that this atom is further divided into parts;
rather, the two directions themselves are the parts.
As for the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "there are directions but no parts, and there are no further subtle divisions," [it means as follows].
Because it is compared and matched according to its characteristics, it is said to have "direction" (method);
yet because it cannot be further dismantled, it is said to be "without division.
If one were to dismantle it further, the mind would instead produce an interpretation of emptiness, thereby transforming into a semblance of the mark of emptiness.
The fourth phrase is missing.

Regarding the question, "Do the five consciousnesses not have a basis and an object?"—that is, among the twenty-five kinds of form, do the five consciousnesses take the conventional as their object or the substantial form? There are two interpretations.
One view holds that the five consciousnesses take the real as their object and do not take the conventional (*prajñapti*) as their object;
the conventional is apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Objection: Real form (*rūpa*) is taken as an object by the five consciousnesses;
it is subsumed within this sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
"Conventional form (*prajñaptirūpa*) is apprehended solely by the mind;

it is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) when confronting the sense faculties. The commentary explains: "According to the intent of the treatise, because it takes the conventional as its object, this may be included within the sphere of mental objects.

However, since it subsumes the conventional according to the real, it is here subsumed under the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, it is asked: 'Do the five consciousnesses not take the conventional as their object?'"
Question: Colors such as long and short are not apprehended by the eye;

since tactile objects such as roughness and smoothness are likewise provisional constructs, they too should not be apprehended by body-consciousness. Answer: Colors such as long and short are distinguished through mutual comparison.
Therefore, it is not apprehended by visual consciousness;

because the various tactile states such as roughness are conventionally designated based on their causal conditions, they are apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Alternatively, like other conventional forms (*prajñaptirūpa*), they are apprehended solely by the mental faculty (*manas*).
Second, the explanation that [consciousness] universally takes both the provisional and the real as its objects:
when the five consciousnesses take the real as their object, the provisional necessarily depends upon the real;
therefore, at the time they take the real as their object, they also take the provisional as their object. If this is so, how does this differ from the Sautrāntika school?
To refute that position, the answer is: first, when the five consciousnesses apprehend length or shortness, they do not separate from the actual color such as blue;
thus, the conventional and the real are combined.

Because those are merely nominal forms, they are not among the five objective spheres (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, it is explained that the objects external to the mind as asserted by the Sautrāntikas are merely nominal,
because they do not function as conditions (*pratyaya*).
Since the Mahāyāna does not depart from consciousness,
the two schools differ naturally;
for the Mahāyāna, in relation to its own reality, length and so forth in physical form are not true.

Since external forms are manifested and yet remain real, it is not prohibited that the five consciousnesses also apprehend their principles (*tattva*). If this is so, how can the five consciousnesses be said to apprehend objects of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The answer is: there are three kinds of specific characteristics.
First is the self-characteristic of the bases (*āyatana*),
which refers to the distinctness of each of the twelve bases.
Second is the self-characteristic of the entities (*vastu*).
Because various colors are distinct within a single location,
there are three types of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa): specifically,
taking blue color and analyzing it down to its ultimate limit, the single atom (paramāṇu).

Now, speaking from the perspective of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction. If that is so, how is it that the five consciousnesses apprehend objects of their own nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), yet are said to be "objects of nature" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) rather than "conforming to the mind"? One should consider this as also being an object of its own nature. Question: If the five consciousnesses were to take conventional (*prajñapti*) entities as their objects...
Why does the auditory consciousness not take the teaching as its object?
If it were admitted that it does so,
then the sense organ would have to confront the object directly.
Names and phrases should not be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
If they were not objects of cognition,
then visual consciousness would likewise not take length and so forth as its objects.
Because both are conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, if qualities such as long and short were not objects of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), they would have to be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Answer: Although forms such as long and short are indeed apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), [they are still perceived by the eye].

Because the provisional follows the real, it does not reside within the locus of dharmas. Furthermore, it is explained that names and so forth are provisionally established based on sound; they are neither identical to nor separate from sound, as the ear does not perceive them [directly].
Length and so forth depend on form; they are themselves form.

Question: Although these are conventional forms, they are apprehended by visual consciousness. One asks: since names and so forth are conventionalities based on sound, why are they neither identical to nor separate from sound?

Yet, since dimensions such as length are conventionalities based on form, why are they not likewise neither identical to nor separate from form? Answer: Dimensions such as length are established through mutual comparison; because they depend upon form, they are not separate from it. They are not, however, identical to it.
Names and so forth are neither identical with nor distinct from their bases because they are merely conventional designations that do not mutually condition one another.

Since names and so forth are established as mere conventional designations upon the basis of conventional sounds—which themselves are already complex and conventional—they are doubly conventional; therefore, they are not the same as [physical qualities] such as length.
This interpretation contradicts what is stated in the second [section] below.
That passage states that speech itself is the expressive agent;
this is not the case here.
That text excludes [the view of] difference.
Language is that which expresses; this is stated according to our own school’s tenet. Thus, the bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and words (*śabdāyatana*) are distinct.
